title: Jeremiah 14:17–22
context: The LORD gives Jeremiah a word of weeping over the broken people, the slain, and the starving. Then a voice, likely the people or the prophet speaking with them, asks whether God has utterly rejected Judah, confesses the sins of the present and past generations, and appeals to God’s name and covenant, closing with trust that the LORD alone gives rain. Speaker shifts in this section are not always marked. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about lament, confession, and hope.

verses.text: “You shall say this word to them: “ ‘Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease; for the virgin daughter of my people is broken with a great breach, with a very grievous wound.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Jeremiah to speak this word: let my eyes run with tears night and day, for my people is broken with a grievous wound. The prophet weeps.

Arminian readers see grief shared between God’s word and the prophet’s heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Whether the tears are the prophet’s, God’s, or both is debated; the words are given as the LORD’s word for Jeremiah to speak.

Reformed readers see sorrow over judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear it pastorally.

verses.text: If I go out into the field, then behold, the slain with the sword! If I enter into the city, then behold, those who are sick with famine! For both the prophet and the priest go about in the land, and have no knowledge.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
In the field are the slain by the sword, in the city those sick with famine, and prophet and priest wander without knowledge. Devastation is everywhere.

Arminian readers see the consequences of rejecting God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The last line is difficult; it may describe leaders wandering in confusion or going into exile, and translations vary.

Reformed readers see leaders failing their people. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground and hold the sense of the last line tentatively.

verses.text: Have you utterly rejected Judah? Has your soul loathed Zion? Why have you struck us, and there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; and for a time of healing, and behold, dismay!
verses.arminianNotes:
The people, or the prophet with them, ask whether God has utterly rejected Judah and loathed Zion, why he has struck them without healing, and why peace has not come. The lament is raw.

Arminian readers see honest prayer in desperate times.
verses.reformedNotes:
The voice is likely the people or Jeremiah praying for them, though the text does not say. The hope of peace echoes the false prophets’ promise (14:13).

Reformed readers see faith crying out. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: We acknowledge, LORD, our wickedness, and the iniquity of our fathers; for we have sinned against you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The speaker acknowledges the people’s wickedness and the iniquity of their fathers: we have sinned against you. Confession deepens.

Arminian readers see repentance that owns both personal and inherited guilt, freely confessed before God (compare the box at Joshua 10:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
The confession links the present generation with its ancestors’ sins.

Reformed readers see honest acknowledgment of sin as the beginning of true prayer. Both traditions read this as shared ground about confession that does not excuse or minimize.

verses.text: Do not abhor us, for your name’s sake. Do not disgrace the throne of your glory. Remember, and don’t break your covenant with us.
verses.arminianNotes:
The speaker asks God not to abhor them for his name’s sake, not to disgrace the throne of his glory, and to remember his covenant. The appeal rests on God.

Arminian readers see prayer appealing to God’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘the throne of your glory’ probably refers to Jerusalem or the temple, though the phrase is not explained.

Reformed readers see the covenant as the ground of hope. Both traditions read this as shared ground about prayer grounded in God’s name and promises.

verses.text: Are there any among the vanities of the nations that can cause rain? Or can the sky give showers? Aren’t you he, the LORD our God? Therefore we will wait for you; for you have made all these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
The speaker asks whether any idol can bring rain or the sky give showers by itself, confessing that the LORD alone made all things: therefore we will wait for you. The prayer ends in trust.

Arminian readers see faith turning from idols.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question returns to the drought of 14:1–6 and answers it with a confession of God as Creator.

Reformed readers see God alone as provider. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.
